questions.q: What does a stalled Distribution Agent typically look like in Replication Monitor, per this lesson?
options: Pending command count keeps climbing for one subscriber while the Log Reader Agent continues working normally
The distribution database disappears entirely
The publisher stops accepting any new transactions
All subscribers immediately show identical error messages
questions.explain: A stalled Distribution Agent means delivery to a specific subscriber isn't progressing, while log capture on the publisher continues fine.

questions.q: What is identity range exhaustion, per this lesson?
options: A server's assigned non-overlapping identity range for a replicated IDENTITY column runs out, causing inserts to fail
The distribution database running out of disk space
A subscriber running out of available table names
The publisher's transaction log filling up completely
questions.explain: SQL Server can assign separate identity ranges to publisher and subscribers to avoid collisions; when a range runs out, inserts at that server start failing.

questions.q: Why can a schema change silently break replication, per this lesson?
options: Replication only knows the article's structure as captured/resynchronized, so plain DDL on a published table can desync publisher and subscriber schema
Schema changes are always automatically propagated with no risk
Replication doesn't support any tables with schemas
Schema changes only affect merge replication, never transactional replication
questions.explain: Without going through a replication-aware path, DDL changes on a published table can leave the subscriber's table shape mismatched with what's being delivered.

questions.q: What's the replication-aware way to handle a schema change on a published table, per this lesson?
options: Use supported procedures like sp_repladdcolumn/sp_repldropcolumn or a supported ALTER TABLE propagation path, rather than routine DDL
Drop and recreate the entire publication every time any column changes
There is no safe way; published tables can never have schema changes
Disable the Distribution Agent permanently before any schema change
questions.explain: SQL Server provides replication-aware procedures and paths specifically to keep publisher and subscriber schema in sync through changes.

questions.q: What common thread connects all three failure modes in this lesson?
options: Publisher and subscriber are loosely coupled, independent systems, and nothing keeps them in sync automatically without active replication maintenance
All three are caused exclusively by network outages
All three only happen in merge replication, never transactional
All three are resolved by simply restarting SQL Server
questions.explain: Because publisher and subscriber are independent systems connected only by the agents and distribution queue, sync has to be actively maintained rather than assumed.
